question: A 52-year-old man with a 2-week history of back pain now presents with sudden urinary retention, bilateral leg weakness, and perineal numbness ('saddle anaesthesia'). What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?

answers.text: Start high-dose oral NSAIDs and arrange MRI within 2–4 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is dangerous. Delay in treating cauda equina syndrome leads to permanent bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction. Waiting weeks for MRI is unacceptable.
Conservative management has no role when cauda equina syndrome is suspected. Neurological deficit from bladder/bowel involvement demands emergency imaging and surgical decompression.

answers.text: Urgent (same-day) MRI lumbar spine and immediate surgical referral for emergency decompression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cauda equina syndrome (urinary retention + bilateral leg weakness + saddle anaesthesia) is a surgical emergency. Functional recovery of the sphincter is time-dependent — decompression within 24–48 hours substantially improves outcomes. MRI confirms the level and extent.

answers.text: Perform a plain X-ray to assess disc space narrowing and then decide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plain X-ray cannot show soft-tissue cauda equina compression. MRI is mandatory. Any delay investigation in this clinical picture is inappropriate.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cauda equina syndrome is a true orthopaedic emergency. The cardinal features are urinary retention (or incontinence), perianal/saddle anaesthesia, and bilateral leg weakness. Same-day MRI and emergency surgical decompression are mandatory — delay risks permanent incontinence and paralysis.

Excellent. Cauda equina syndrome = urinary retention + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral leg weakness → EMERGENCY. MRI same day + urgent surgical decompression. This presentation should never be sent home.
